The stabilization measures help protect the San Francisquito Creek Railroad Bridge and the Alma Street Pedestrian and Bicycle Bridge by reducing erosion and strengthening the creek banks against future storm impacts.Caltrain owns and maintains the railroad bridge located between Menlo Park and Palo Alto. In 2023, severe winter storms caused significant erosion along the creek banks, threatening the stability of the ground supporting these bridges. In coordination with the San Francisquito Creek Joint Powers Authority (SFCJPA), Caltrain implemented emergency temporary bank stabilization measures in November 2023 to address the immediate erosion concerns. The current project provides long-term creek bank stabilization and erosion protection, enhancing the resilience of both bridges and helping protect the historic El Palo Alto tree against future storm impacts. Key construction activities included: Temporary creek diversion and shoringCreek bank excavation and grading Installation of vegetated boulder revetmentConstruction of vegetated soil-wrapped liftsReplacement of the Menlo Park storm drain outfall with a backflow prevention device Riparian habitat restoration through invasive vegetation removal and native plantingsThe in-stream stabilization work was completed on September 23, three weeks ahead of the October 15 deadline established by environmental regulators from the US Army Corps of Engineers, California Department of Fish and Wildlife and the Regional Water Quality Control Board. This early completion marks a significant milestone for Caltrain’s Capital Delivery Program, strengthening critical infrastructure ahead of the anticipated severe winter storm season. Remaining landscaping and irrigation installation activities are underway and expected to be completed by the end of November.  “As El Niño approaches, we’re making sure our infrastructure is ready to weather the storm,” said Caltrain Executive Director Michelle Bouchard. “Stabilizing the creek and protecting our bridge will help us keep service running safely and on time.”“The SFCJPA is pleased to see this important bank stabilization project successfully completed, and we congratulate Caltrain on reaching this milestone,” said SFCJPA Board Chair Greer Stone. “With the potential for El Niño to bring significant winter storms to our region, the timing of this work could not be more important. Strengthening this critical section of San Francisquito Creek will help reduce the risk of erosion and flooding and improve the resilience of communities along the creek as we prepare for the rainy season.”Forecasters expect the weather pattern to continue to strengthen, causing flooding and related storm impacts along the entire West Coast. Last month, Governor Gavin Newsom proclaimed a state of emergency ahead of the emerging El Niño storm season. The San Francisquito Creek Bank Stabilization Project is a partnership between Caltrain and the Cities of Menlo Park and Palo Alto to reinforce and restore a permanent creek embankment. The project budget was $14 million, with the city of Palo Alto contributing $1.06 million and the city of Menlo Park contributing $1.16 million.###About Caltrain: Owned and operated by the Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board, Caltrain provides rail service from San Francisco to San Jose, with commute service to Gilroy. This has allowed Caltrain to return 23% of its electricity to the grid, resulting in SJCE and WestLight Energy paying the rail agency $1 million annually.“Since September 2024, every single one of our trains carrying passengers between San Francisco and San Jose have run on 100% renewable green energy generated right here in the state of California,” said Caltrain Executive Director Michelle Bouchard. “Electrifying Caltrain was an investment in future generations that will continue to pay out for decades to come.”“On Clean Air Day, we’re celebrating what clean energy looks like in action: electric trains replacing diesel, renewable electricity powering the ride, and fewer emissions in the communities along the corridor. Overall satisfaction held at 4.40 out of 5, up from 4.02 in 2024, the final survey taken before Caltrain launched electrified service.Caltrain riders report broad satisfaction across multiple survey categories. The onboard experience scored 4.45, stations scored 4.32, and riders' sense of safety on Caltrain climbed to 4.44, up from 4.23 in 2024. On-time arrival at riders' destinations scored 4.40, and the accuracy of arrival times on platform signs scored 4.38. Caltrain conductors stood out in particular, with conductors' politeness and helpfulness rated at 4.63, the highest score conductors have received in the survey's history, and gave conductors' professional appearance a 4.70 in the first year that question was asked."Our riders noticed the difference electrification made on day one, and two years later they're telling us those improvements have reinvented their experience for the better," said Caltrain Executive Director Michelle Bouchard. "Those ratings belong to the conductors, the maintenance crews, and the operations staff who show up every day to run a safe railroad people want to ride and that the whole Bay Area can be proud of. We will continue to strive to provide the reliable, frequent service that our riders rate so highly while we engage in contingency planning to address our impending fiscal cliff, which may require a reduction in service."The survey shows how much Caltrain's rider base has changed and how the agency continues to adapt to shifting ridership patterns. Caltrain now serves an estimated 49,000 unique riders each month, roughly 37,000 more than in 2021 and close to its 2019 total, even though fewer riders now commute five days a week. The average rider takes the train two to three times a week, and special events have become a major ridership source that the agency is targeting with outreach and marketing efforts. The increase in special event ridership has been supplemented by Caltrain’s half-hourly service-with even more service at peak hours-making it more convenient than ever before to take Caltrain. 1 in 5 riders said they took their first Caltrain trip to attend a game, concert, or festival. Riders who travel to events reported the same 4.4 satisfaction as riders overall.Riders are also coming back in growing numbers. Caltrain carried 12.6 million riders in fiscal year 2026, up 37.6% from the year before, building on being named the fastest-growing transit agency in the country in 2025 by the American Public Transportation Association (APTA). Since electrification, Caltrain’s improved service,  average weekend ridership climbed 40.1% in FY2026 to 21,210. Weekday ridership rose 37.5%, and July set a new high of 1.32 million riders in a single month.APTA has awarded Caltrain with its Outstanding Public Transportation System Achievement Award for 2026.Those gains come as Caltrain, like transit agencies across the Bay Area, faces a structural operating deficit as remote and hybrid work continue to reshape commuting. Caltrain has responded on three fronts: cutting costs, generating new revenue from advertising, property, and other assets, and adapting its service to attract new riders. Despite Caltrain cutting $76 million in costs over the last five years, the increase in ridership and fare revenue is insufficient to close the funding gap, and additional external funding is needed to maintain current levels of service.    The survey drew responses from 2,631 riders on randomly selected weekday and weekend trains and carries a margin of error of 1.78%.The survey was presented to the Caltrain Board of Directors on October 1.
